meta.title: Dangerous Munitions Near Me
meta.timezone_note: Dates and 'last checked' values are recorded in America/Phoenix (UTC-7) calendar dates unless a source gives another zone.
meta.inclusion_rule: Includes every clearly named military/DoD facility on EPA's current OB/OD list as of the March 11, 2025 table (page also marked July 14, 2026), plus JMC conventional demil hubs named in the Oct 1, 2025 Hrycak briefing when they map to those facilities, plus Camp Minden, Savanna Army Depot, and Lake City Army Ammunition Plant. Commercial explosives plants, DOE sites, NASA Wallops, and the Saipan DFEMS entry on the same EPA list are omitted from this draft pending a later decision.
meta.coordinate_policy: Latitude and longitude are EPA FRS LATITUDE83/LONGITUDE83 for the site's RCRA ID when available. Collection method and accuracy are recorded when FRS provides them. Coordinates are not guessed or manually offset.
meta.verification_policy: verified: the listed facts were confirmed from official or other allowed primary sources. partly verified: official identity (and usually the EPA listing or a documented incident) is confirmed, but inventory, current operations, or some incident details remain incomplete. unverified: a claim was recorded but not confirmed against a primary source. Blank fields mean no source, not a zero or a no.
meta.source_exclusions: This draft does not cite NYT, CNN, MSNBC/MS NOW, Fox News, Snopes, or PolitiFact.

sites.name: Redstone Arsenal
sites.coordinate_method: UNKNOWN
sites.known_energetics: ADEM's June 2026 draft-modification fact sheet says Redstone is a U.S. Army Aviation and Missile Command installation. The OB/OD area is used to burn and detonate hazardous energetic waste with the characteristic of reactivity (D003) and explosiveness. The open-burning area consists of five burn pans on concrete pads; open detonation takes place in a designated OD area. Explosive Destruction System (EDS) units are used to treat recovered munitions or other items. This draft does not have a current item-level inventory.
sites.current_status: Listed on EPA's current OB/OD facilities table as permitted, with a listed expiration of July 18, 2031. ADEM issued a 10-year hazardous-waste permit renewal effective July 19, 2021 (EPA ID AL7210020742 / AL 7 210 020 742). ADEM published a draft permit modification fact sheet for public comment June 3–July 20, 2026, to incorporate investigations and corrective measures approved since the last modification (August 8, 2022). This draft did not independently confirm whether that 2026 modification was finalized.

notable_incidents.summary: Redstone Arsenal Public Affairs: at about 8:45 a.m., a fire and explosion occurred at Building 7352, an Aviation and Missile Research, Development, and Engineering Center facility, during demilitarization operations involving ammonium perchlorate, an oxidizer used in solid rocket propellant. Two AMRDEC contractors were injured and taken to UAB's Burn Center; a third employee nearby was not injured. There were no fatalities.

sites.notes: The 2010 event was a production/demil-building accident, not a documented aging-drum storage emergency. Current energetic holdings were not inventoried in this pass.

sites.name: Navy Region Hawaii – Waipio Peninsula
sites.coordinate_method: GDT-ADDRESS MATCHING (GEOCODING), reference: ENTRANCE POINT OF A FACILITY OR STATION
sites.known_energetics: The site is used to treat remediation-waste munitions recovered from dredging and construction-related activities at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam. A July 11, 2015 Navy release said recovered types from Pearl Harbor dredged-material screening included 5-inch projectiles, 4.5-inch barrage rockets and/or motors, 3-inch and 75mm projectiles, 60mm mortars, 40mm and 20mm projectiles and/or casings, grenades, a practice bomb, a TNT demolition charge, fuzes, and small-arms ammunition. A Hawaii Department of Health public notice dated August 15, 2024, on a draft five-year Remedial Action Plan permit renewal, would limit each detonation shot to no more than 16 pounds net explosive weight unless DOH approves a larger shot, and would cap annual treatment at 5,760 pounds net explosive weight per 365-day period. Those numeric limits are from the 2024 draft public notice, not from a final permit page retrieved in this pass.
sites.current_status: Listed on EPA's current OB/OD facilities table as permitted, with a listed expiration of January 29, 2029. Hawaii DOH solicited public comment beginning August 15, 2024, on a draft five-year RAP permit renewal for continued controlled intentional detonations at the Waipio Peninsula Annex. This draft did not independently retrieve a final 2024–2025 RAP issuance. In 2015, DOH granted a 90-day State Emergency Hazardous Waste Permit on June 29, 2015, allowing up to 50 detonation events and no more than 15 pounds net explosive weight per event, to destroy munitions recovered from dredged material.

notable_incidents.summary: Navy Region Hawaii announced scheduled controlled detonations July 14–31, 2015 (work had also occurred July 7–8) at the Confined Disposal Facility on Waipio Peninsula to destroy munitions recovered from screening of Pearl Harbor dredged material, under the June 29, 2015 emergency permit. The Navy said the project had previously treated some recovered munitions on Oct. 30, 2013, was suspended, and resumed in May 2015.

sites.notes: These operations are permitted treatment of recovered munitions, not a spontaneous storage explosion. Whether the August 2024 draft RAP was finalized was not confirmed in this pass.

sites.name: Iowa Army Ammunition Plant
sites.known_energetics: Bulk lead azide stored wetted in 68 55-gallon plastic drums in two earth-covered magazines; Col. Aaron C. Teller (71st Ordnance Group EOD) states the total weight is 9,773.5 lb. The plant also has a conventional munitions load-assemble-pack mission. This draft does not inventory other energetics on site.
sites.current_status: As of Nov 23, 2026 (America/Phoenix): the planned in-place detonation had not occurred. The original date was Nov 20; the Army postponed to Nov 23, then announced Nov 25. The Eighth Circuit issued an administrative stay of EPA's emergency treatment permit on Nov 19, pending a ruling on the emergency stay motion in No. 26-3374; as of a CourtListener docket review on Nov 23, that merits ruling had not issued. Iowa Public Radio reported that President Trump posted on Truth Social on Nov 23 that he ordered the military not to proceed until the Eighth Circuit agrees they can go forward, and subject to Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing. IAAAP also holds a regular RCRA OB/OD permit (EPA ID IA7213820445) listed as permitted through Sept 28, 2028. The emergency permit for in-place magazine detonation is a separate authorization, issued Nov 13, 2026, effective through Feb 11, 2027.

notable_incidents.summary: Army plan to destroy 68 drums of crystallized, unserviceable lead azide by controlled in-place detonation in two earth-covered magazines. EPA issued an emergency RCRA permit on Nov 13, 2026. The shot did not take place on Nov 20 or Nov 23, 2026, and remained subject to a court stay and a reported presidential stand-down order.

sites.notes: The closest documented historical analog for bulk lead azide in deteriorating 55-gallon drums is Savanna Army Depot (1984). A March 21, 2014 Army article attributed DoD's 2004 green-primaries work to concern over a 40-year-old deteriorating lead azide stockpile at IAAAP. A separate research log kept with this draft has the claim-by-claim review.

sites.name: Savanna Army Depot Activity
sites.coordinate_method: GDT-ADDRESS MATCHING (GEOCODING); reference: entrance point of a facility or station. FRS also lists a SEMS point at 42.21, -90.313331; this draft uses the RCRA record and does not average the two.
sites.permit_status: Not on EPA's current OB/OD operating list
sites.known_energetics: William Shaneyfelt, safety officer at Savanna Army Depot Activity, described Vietnam-era surplus bulk lead azide in deteriorating 55-gallon drums in a 1984 paper to the DoD Explosives Safety Board. Electrolysis destroyed about half the stockpile; the remainder was repacked. The public record reviewed for this draft does not establish what happened to the remaining drums after 1984.
sites.current_status: A former Army depot. Official Army BRAC records recommend closing Savanna Army Depot Activity and relocating the U.S. Army Defense Ammunition Center and School to McAlester Army Ammunition Plant, Oklahoma. An Army BRAC NEPA public document states that SVADA ceased operations and officially closed on May 20, 2000. The depot was listed on the EPA National Priorities List on October 15, 1984. Parcel conveyance has continued; a DENIX page updated July 15, 2026, lists starting acreage of 12,884.32, conveyed 5,363.76, and remaining 7,520.56, with current owners including USFWS, USACE, Illinois DNR, and the Jo-Carroll Depot Local Redevelopment Authority. The installation is not on EPA's current OB/OD operating list. This draft still has not found an official document that accounts for the remaining bulk lead azide drums after the 1984 repack — including whether they were later destroyed, sold, or transferred (for example when the ammunition school moved to McAlester). A 1990 USADACS paper presented from Savanna discusses electrochemical reduction as a process demonstrated on lead azide, but it does not state the fate of the remaining 1984 stockpile.

notable_incidents.summary: Shaneyfelt paper (21st Explosives Safety Seminar, Houston, Aug 28–30, 1984): surplus bulk lead azide in deteriorating drums; sale attempts failed; electrolytic destruction halted after about half the stockpile; remaining leaking drums were repacked. The paper also describes a process-building contamination accident in which sodium azide washdown reacted with brass/copper debris and caused a 'loud, though not extremely dangerous, explosion.' That event was not a storage-drum detonation.

sites.notes: Closest documented historical analog to IAAAP's bulk lead azide drums. Depot closed May 20, 2000. The post-1984 fate of the remaining lead azide remains a research gap; no official destruction or transfer record for that residual stockpile was found in this pass.

sites.known_energetics: M6 propellant and clean-burning igniter (CBI) left from Explo Systems contractor storage of Army-origin material. These are HD 1.3 propellant/igniter materials, not primary explosives such as lead azide. A Louisiana National Guard release dated April 21, 2017, said the State of Louisiana contracted Explosive Service International on June 17, 2015, to destroy approximately 15,687,247 pounds of M6 and approximately 320,890 pounds of CBI, and that destruction of the M6 and CBI had been successfully completed in accordance with the contract. The Minden Press-Herald reported on October 24, 2018, that 15 pounds of M6 remained in a bunker thought too unstable to move. This draft did not find an official 2019–2026 confirmation that those 15 pounds were later destroyed.
sites.current_status: The main contained-burn disposal campaign was declared complete by the Louisiana National Guard on April 21, 2017; ESI was then to conduct about 30 days of cleanup, including burning residual debris, after which the chamber would not be used in that capacity again at Camp Minden. As of an October 24, 2018, Minden Press-Herald account of a Camp Minden Citizens Advisory Group meeting, 15 pounds of M6 were still reported in a bunker, the burn chamber was no longer in use and was up for sale, and Louisiana Military Department project coordinator Winston Matejowsky was quoted saying closure could not go on until that M6 was burned. This draft has not independently confirmed, from an official 2019–2026 source, whether those 15 pounds remain, were burned, or were otherwise disposed of.

notable_incidents.summary: Explosion of a magazine at Explo Systems, Camp Minden. EPA chronology: Louisiana State Police later identified about 10 million pounds of unsecured M6; the town of Doyline (about 400 homes) was evacuated during operational hours.

Army Explosives Safety Board report cited in the EPA chronology: the probability of an explosives event related to long-term storage of M6 at Camp Minden was 'likely'; the Board recommended open burn/open detonation within two years.
EPA approved a contained-burn system after tests showed 99.99% destruction of chemicals of concern, for about 16 million pounds of M6 and CBI.

About 120,960 pounds of CBI auto-ignited in an earth-covered magazine and destroyed the bunker. Louisiana National Guard reported no injuries. An Army Explosive Safety Technical Assistance Visit then advised that remaining CBI was too dangerous to handle and should be destroyed in place, with some magazines remotely ignited because entering them was not acceptable.

Louisiana National Guard announced that destruction of approximately 15,687,247 pounds of M6 propellant and approximately 320,890 pounds of CBI had been successfully completed under the June 17, 2015, contract with Explosive Service International. Cleanup of residual debris was expected to take about 30 days.

Minden Press-Herald, reporting on a Camp Minden Citizens Advisory Group meeting: 15 pounds of M6 propellant remained in a bunker thought too unstable to move; the burn chamber was no longer in use and was up for sale; LMD project coordinator Winston Matejowsky was quoted saying the leftover should have been taken care of along the way and that the longer it was held the more likely it was to self-ignite. This draft did not find a later official confirmation of disposal.

sites.notes: Closest recent official parallel to IAAAP's 'cannot safely move it, destroy in place' finding, though the chemistry differs. The main tonnage was officially declared destroyed in April 2017; a reported 15-pound leftover in October 2018 is the remaining residual-holdings gap.

sites.known_energetics: A May 20, 2022 Maryland Department of the Environment tentative-determination fact sheet and draft Controlled Hazardous Substance permit A-190 (EPA ID MD3210021355) describe these treatment units: the J-Field Open Detonation unit, for waste conventional explosives and munitions (and items fully decontaminated or formally found not to contain lethal agents); and Old Bombing Field open-burn and open-detonation units, used to treat waste conventional explosives and propellants, with open burning of waste propellants on steel pans and open detonation in a designated 18.4-acre site. The draft also lists other Edgewood Area hazardous-waste units operated by DEVCOM Chemical Biological Center and related organizations (storage, thermal treatment, Explosive Destruction System, Munitions Assessment and Processing System). Those descriptions are from the 2022 draft renewal, not from a retrieved final signed 2022–2026 permit. Separately, a 2024 emergency permit addressed about 35 pounds of potentially unstable TMETN at an Army Research Laboratory bunker.
sites.current_status: MDE received a renewal application for CHS permit A-190 on August 14, 2019, which is before the February 15, 2020 expiration of the prior term. On May 20, 2022, MDE issued a tentative determination to renew the permit, with a draft 10-year permit. Maryland open-data records reviewed in this pass still listed permit A-190 as expired (term February 15, 2010–February 15, 2020) and not administratively extended. EPA's current OB/OD list, last updated March 11, 2025, still shows the facility as permitted with the February 15, 2020 expiration. This draft did not retrieve a final post-2022 signed CHS permit. Because the renewal application was received before expiration, the 40 CFR 270.51 continuation rule may apply, but a final issuance was not confirmed here.

notable_incidents.summary: MDE temporary emergency permit E2024-1 (oral approval November 21, 2024; written permit November 22, 2024; expired February 19, 2025) authorized on-site contained chemical treatment of approximately 35 pounds of trimethylolethane trinitrate (TMETN, CAS 3032-55-1) in a single container at Army Research Laboratory Bunker 1174 on Spesutie Island. Army explosives-safety experts were concerned the material may have become unstable after about 10 years of storage and might detonate if shipped. ARL proposed chemical neutralization by MuniRem Environmental, LLC, as an alternative to open detonation. The permit states there was no other TMETN on the inventory list.

sites.notes: The 2024 TMETN action is a small-quantity instability case treated by proposed chemical neutralization under an emergency permit, not a bulk-drum detonation. Whether the work was completed, and whether CHS permit A-190 was finally renewed, were not independently confirmed.

sites.name: Lone Star Army Ammunition Plant
sites.known_energetics: An official Army BRAC installation report (updated November 3, 2025; compilation updated January 23, 2026) says Lone Star Army Ammunition Plant performed a load-assemble-pack munitions production mission for more than 60 years on 11 production lines. The 2005 BRAC Commission recommended relocating storage and demilitarization functions to McAlester AAP; 105mm and 155mm ICM artillery, MLRS artillery, hand grenades, and 60mm and 81mm mortars to Milan AAP; mines and detonators/relays/delays functions to Iowa AAP; and demolition-charges functions to Crane Army Ammunition Activity. That official relocation of detonator functions to IAAAP is not, by itself, a documented origin for IAAAP's 2026 lead azide drums. Day & Zimmermann–Lone Star remains the Army's agent for two RCRA-regulated units, the High Explosives Burning Ground and the High Explosives Demolition Ground. EPA lists this EPA ID (TXR000084774) separately from Day & Zimmermann Lone Star Facility (TXR000080174).
sites.current_status: The same official BRAC report states that all active missions ceased and the plant closed as part of BRAC 2005 on September 30, 2009. A staff of two federal employees remain for caretaker oversight; caretaker operations are executed by Day & Zimmermann–Lone Star under a cost-plus caretaker contract. As of the November 3, 2025 update, 14,292 of 15,589 acres had been conveyed; 1,297 acres remained, with conveyance depending on cleanup. The site is on the National Priorities List. EPA's current OB/OD list still shows Lone Star Army Ammunition Plant as permitted, with a listed expiration of January 16, 2031.
sites.notes: Closed production plant under BRAC caretaker and cleanup; remaining RCRA OB/OD units are in caretaker/agent status. This draft does not claim that IAAAP's 68 drums came from Lone Star.

sites.name: Naval Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren
sites.known_energetics: Virginia DEQ hazardous-waste permit issued to the United States Navy authorizes treatment of hazardous waste by open burning and open detonation at the Naval Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren Site (Churchill Range plans are among the permit attachments). This draft does not record a complete item-level list from the permit attachments. The facility is a Navy weapons-development and test activity; a current inventory of energetics in storage was not retrieved.
sites.current_status: The Virginia DEQ permit is effective as of April 28, 2021, and remains in effect until April 28, 2031, unless revoked, reissued, or terminated. EPA's current OB/OD list shows the facility as permitted with that April 28, 2031 expiration.
sites.notes: Basic entry from the EPA OB/OD list and FRS coordinates only. Incidents and energetics inventory need research.

sites.name: Radford Army Ammunition Plant
sites.coordinate_method: CLASSICAL SURVEYING TECHNIQUES, accuracy_value=1, reference: UNKNOWN
sites.known_energetics: A production plant for energetic materials, including nitrocellulose (the material named in coverage of the June 2018 flash fire). This draft does not have a full current product inventory.
sites.current_status: Listed on EPA's current OB/OD facilities table as permitted, with a listed expiration of Sept 17, 2031. It is a production plant, not a JMC conventional-demil hub in the Oct 1, 2025 briefing.

notable_incidents.summary: AP reported a nitrocellulose flash fire at Radford Army Ammunition Plant that injured three workers. This was a production accident, not an aging-drum storage emergency. This draft did not independently retrieve the full AP article body (Cloudflare block during collection).

sites.notes: Local outlets also covered the 2018 fire and later reported that one of the injured workers, Andrew Goad, died of his injuries. That fatality was not independently confirmed from AP in this pass.
